name: Mara Tev
life: Mara became a dispatcher after losing a thumb joint in a luggage door. She understands the small indignity of a job being taken away piece by piece. Retiring a callsign deserves more ceremony than clearing a screen. Saturday often includes a stop at the foot of Harbor Viaduct, where Mara pauses where the machinery overhead makes two people stand close enough to hear each other.
voice: His callsign has been on my board since I joined. I took it off and put it on the passenger booking. I want the younger drivers to hear how a farewell sounds on the radio.
appearance: Mara has a high puff tied with plain cord, a softly rounded chin under sharp cheekbones, and a favorite piece of clothing, a pale blue work shirt. It usually goes with a tiny red thread tied through the lowest buttonhole. When somebody else has the floor, Mara touches a knuckle to the chin when searching for a word.
personality: Mara can be wonderfully decisive about an emergency and maddeningly undecided about a gift. This is because a person can say precisely what hurts and rarely says exactly what they want.
agenda: To turn the old callsign into a final passenger booking.
family: Leon White is Mara’s cousin. Mara puts the kettle on. Leon chooses the music. The cups come out before either brings up the reason for the visit. They trust a difficult conversation more if it has had an ordinary beginning. Asked about *The absent signature*, Leon says, “I used the berth for pocket money and never asked whose money repaired it.”
connections: Carmen Saye. The retired callsign gives the payroll worker a way to book a last trip before drawing routes for the bus.

reactions.situation: If a neighbor offers a costly present
reactions.response: Mara asks for an afternoon to work out whether accepting it would put someone else in debt.
